intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.1.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we present six affected individuals from six unrelated families, carrying bi-allelic GAD1 variants, presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
checks.explanation: The paper reports homozygous variants in five families and compound heterozygous variants in one, causing DEE. The 'DEE89' label is OMIM nomenclature and does not appear in the paper.

checks.claim: The GAD1 gene is located on chromosome 2q31.1.
checks.evidence_quote: identification of the variant was based on autozygosity mapping, in which they identified a recessive locus of 5 cM located at 2q24-31.1
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature. The paper places GAD1 within the 2q24-31.1 locus.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder (Chatron et al., 2020). Seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy (Chatron et al., 2020) and are often hard to treat (Neuray et al., 2020). Affected children have severe global developmental delay (Chatron et al., 2020) and hypotonia (Neuray et al., 2020). Some patients also have features outside the nervous system, including cleft palate, skeletal abnormalities such as joint contractures, and omphalocele (Chatron et al., 2020).

checks.claim: DEE89 is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: In all families, Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the GAD1 variants with the disease phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 1) and a recessive mode of inheritance associated with the disease.
checks.explanation: Recessive inheritance stated; disease is a DEE.

checks.claim: In DEE89, seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: Seizure onset occurred in the first 2 months of life in all patients. All 10 patients, from whom early disease history was available, presented with seizure onset in the first month of life

checks.claim: Seizures in DEE89 are often hard to treat.
checks.evidence_quote: Seizures were pharmacologically controlled in three of six affected individuals, with three reported as drug-resistant.
checks.explanation: Only half of the patients (three of six) were drug-resistant, so 'often hard to treat' somewhat overstates a split result.

checks.claim: Children affected with DEE89 have severe global developmental delay.
checks.evidence_quote: All living patients had severe psychomotor delay.

checks.claim: Children affected with DEE89 have hypotonia.
checks.evidence_quote: presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, characterized by early-infantile onset epilepsy and hypotonia
checks.explanation: The paper names hypotonia as a key feature.

checks.claim: Some patients with DEE89 have cleft palate.
checks.evidence_quote: Seven patients presented a cleft palate and two also had an omphalocele

checks.claim: Some patients with DEE89 have skeletal abnormalities such as joint contractures.
checks.evidence_quote: Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus.

checks.claim: Some patients with DEE89 have omphalocele.
checks.evidence_quote: Both patients from Family B presented omphalocele

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 affected individuals from 6 unrelated families with biallelic GAD1 variants. The patients had early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, with seizure onset in the first 2 months of life, and severe developmental impairment. Seven patients had cleft palate, and 2 also had omphalocele. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus. Chatron et al. (2020) described the disorder as a neonatal-onset syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.

checks.evidence_quote: caused by bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in GAD1, as presented by 11 patients from six independent consanguineous families.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of DEE89 in the families reported by Chatron et al. (2020) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of DEE89 in the families reported by Chatron et al. (2020) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: In all families, Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the GAD1 variants with the disease phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 1) and a recessive mode of inheritance associated with the disease.

paragraphs.text: In 11 patients from 6 unrelated families with DEE89, Chatron et al. (2020) identified homozygous variants in the GAD1 gene by whole-exome sequencing (4 families) or whole-genome sequencing (2 families). GAD1 encodes the glutamate decarboxylase enzyme GAD67, which catalyzes the decarboxylation of glutamic acid to form GABA. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variants segregated with the disorder in all families. Chatron et al. (2020) proposed that the disorder results from loss of GAD1 function and reduced GABA synthesis.
